title: The Five Contemplations
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart emphasizes the importance of recognizing our deep connection to all beings and the world around us, encouraging us to cultivate gratitude, generosity, and mindfulness in everyday actions like eating. This understanding allows us to see that our existence is not separate from others, but rather intertwined with their lives and deaths, fostering a sense of equality and compassion. By embracing this interconnectedness, we can transform our relationship with the world and strive to embody the principles of Buddhism, becoming vessels for helping others and realizing our own potential as expressions of the Buddha's way.

sentences.text: Good morning.
Here we are on the 5th of July with summer and sun beckoning.
There are so many things you could do, and yet here you are.
You have chosen to sit and bow and chant.
I am deeply grateful, and I thank you for your dedication to practice.
I had a rather lighthearted talk planned for today on the meal chant.
But as I sat down and started to write it, it just wrote itself and it went in a different direction.
So the talk is actually only about a small portion of the meal chant, which is called the five contemplations.
*We reflect on the effort that brought us this food and consider how it comes to us.
We reflect on our virtue and practice and whether we are worthy of this offering.
We regard it as essential to keep the mind free from excesses such as greed.
We regard this food as good medicine to sustain our life.
For the sake of enlightenment, we now receive this food.*
So my talk begins with a big thank you to all my teachers.
Above all, my gratitude goes to Norman Fischer.
For many years, he has allowed me to be his student.
His encouragement moved me off "stuck" when I barked, and his trust kept me going when I had none of my own.
Thank you, Norman.
I also thank Tim for the many years he's been there for me and that we have been working together.
The aspiration to do the best for the Sangha is always there.
I also appreciate all the other teachers I encountered over the years.
Some of them even wore [unclear: "ropes"], some of them didn't.
To them, I offer:
*Every fruit and flower, every kind of healing draught, and all the precious gems the world contains, with all pure waters of refreshment.
Every mountain [unclear: "rotted"] precious jewels, all sweet and lovely forest groves.
The trees of paradise adorned with blossoms.
Trees with branches bowed [unclear: "was"] perfect fruit.*
That was Shantideva.

And like Shantideva, in those two verses, I wish to shower all my teachers with gifts: [unclear: "ropes"], wish-fulfilling jewels, golden umbrellas, summer and winter palaces, flowers from the mountains.
And maybe this aspiration, the deep and warm desire to give these gifts, is enough.
Dhanaparamita, the perfection of giving, doing what I can right now.
In these times of coronavirus, many experience isolation, missing the opportunity to socialize with friends and loved ones due to the risk it poses to both sides.
We may miss entertainments and events, such as dinner with friends, going to a restaurant, going to the movies or live performances.
I understand there are even people who miss shopping and getting their hair or nails done.
Clubs and groups and sports teams cannot practice together without the risk of making each other sick.
Especially religious organizations are hard hit.
We chant together.
We share physical space in close proximity for hours.
And yet, we have given our time and our hearts to sangha, some of us for many years, some maybe for a few weeks.
It does not make any difference.
Practicing and working together so sangha may flourish.
We love spending time in each other's company.
Lots of time.
Again, in July 2020, that would just mean putting each other at risk.
Also, in any other year, we would have come back from our Samish Island session just a few weeks ago, newly energized through practice, teachings and the presence of sangha.
Instead, we stayed at home, turned on our computers and had an online session.
There was no opportunity to catch up.
How you doing?
No hugs.
No sitting next to people, falling in love with my neighbors every time, like every time during session.
No morning [unclear: "chunno"].
And yet, I don't know about you, but I thought it was great to have this online session.
Old friends, most of them were there, plus some new ones.
There they were, all in their little neat, small squares on my computer screen.
We were all together, always coming home.
The feeling of practice was right there.
One thing I personally missed was sesshin food.
Leaving the zendo at Samish, chanting ho, walking along, watching the herons, swallows, the rabbits, the islands and the seas: wonderful.
I hope that there will be a time when we can return to Samish for sesshin.
But we just don't know, do we?
Change is inevitable.
I am sure that the Church of Christ, just like we, is trying to figure out how to go forward, how to navigate these uncertain waters.
I am sure that for the camp, just like for us, just like for Dogen, who wrote so often in so many ways, practice occurs.
We are uncertain.
And yet we go forward.
It does not always take the form we expect.
The results may totally differ from what we were looking for.
Your mileage may vary.
In our practice, we are advised not to have a gaining mind.
Our current situation drives home another Buddhist teaching, the teaching of Indra's net, a reminder of interconnection, interdependence and interpenetration.
An unknown animal species, a market in China, a virus, human carriers, social isolation, physical distancing, the Zoom app, you and me, Samish, sesshin.
Everything is so closely connected.
We couldn't take it apart, even if we tried.
The Huayang patriarch [unclear: "Duchen"], he lived from 1557 till 640, gives an overview of this concept of Indra's net.
And I apologize upfront, the language is really obtuse, kind of bizarre, repeats itself.
And yet, he knew what he was talking about.
He wrote:
*The manner in which all dharmas interpenetrate is like an imperial net of celestial jewels extending in all directions, infinitely, without limit.
As for the imperial net of heavenly jewels, it is known as Indra's net, a net which is entirely made of jewels.
Because of the clarity of these jewels, they are all reflected in and enter into each other.
Within each jewel simultaneously is reflected the whole net.
Ultimately, nothing comes or goes.
If we pick one specific jewel and examine it closely, it will immediately reflect the image of every other jewel.
The image of each of these jewels within one jewel appearing brilliantly.
None of the other jewels interfere with this.
When one sits within one jewel, one is sitting in all jewels.
How is this so?
Because within each jewel are present all jewels.
The inverse is also understood in the same way.
Just as one goes into one jewel, and thus enters every other jewel while never leaving, so one enters while never leaving this jewel.*
So this is not 21st century language, and it's not our way of thinking.
But if we work on it, it can become so.
We have the choice of shifting our view.
Instead of trying to extricate ourselves and making ourselves and our action singular, let's try this on for size.
Love the connection.
Seeing ourselves mirrored in everything we encounter.
Finding bits and pieces of ourselves in unexpected corners.
The human mind is not built to deal with Indra's net.
It can't.
It's too big.
It's too complex.
However, if we try, we can get in touch with it.
And why am I talking about Indra's net?
Interconnection, gratitude and generosity.
Didn't the announcement say mealchant?
Because the mealchant is nothing but Indra's net, gratitude, and generosity.
Let us hear the five contemplations one more time, with this in mind.
*We reflect on the effort that brought us this food and consider how it comes to us.
We reflect on our virtue and practice and whether we are worthy of this offering.
We regard it as essential to keep the mind free from excesses such as greed.
We regard this food as good medicine to sustain our life.
For the sake of enlightenment, we now receive this food.*
When we are at sesshin, it is not like India in the times of the Buddha, that generous donors cover our expenses and donate our food.
So I might think that I bought this food, that I bought this service, and that this is just the way it's supposed to be.
I ask you, is this really so?
We walk into a grocery store, put food into our shopping cart, give the cashier our credit card and walk out.
I ask you, sit with this.
What did it take for my morning cup of coffee, the bowl of oats with berries and yogurt?
Oats, cows, sun, soil, rain, fire, bees, markets, trucks, water pipes, truck drivers, gas stations, streets, grocery stores, houses for people.
I could go on for the rest of the day, for the rest of my life.
Someone, once upon a time, must have figured out how to tame a cow and turn milk into yogurt.
It was not one person.
Rightly seen, it took the entire universe.
It is a miracle.
It is millions and millions of years of interdependence.
And most importantly, let us not exclude ourselves from the miracle.
Let us not only see miracles looking out, the beauty of it all.
The intricate functioning of our bodies and our minds is stunning.
Well, we might want to say mine isn't working so well today, but just the fact that you can think that and say that is the miracle.
How can we be less when the iron in our blood came from the heart of exploding stars?
How can we feel small?
The oxygen in each and every breath was generated by living things.
Our food is a gift from the network of all beings.
Beings die so we can eat.
That is called being alive.
We don't need to freeze at the thought.
We don't need to starve.
And yet utterly forgetting that beings die so we can live is also not part of our path.
We hold both life and death equally.
Blue Cliff Record, Case 14.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the teaching of a lifetime?"
Yunmen replied, "An appropriate response."
*May our intentions equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
